glance.why: Tianjin is the closest thing China has to a European city centre, because nine foreign powers each built one here between 1860 and 1945 and they are all still standing, side by side along the river. It is also a famously funny city, home to crosstalk comedy and a snack culture Beijingers travel down for. Thirty-five minutes from Beijing by train, and almost nobody goes.
glance.idealStay: 1-2 days, or a day trip from Beijing

history.story: Tianjin's name means the ford of heaven, from the emperor who crossed the river here on his way to seize the throne. It spent centuries as Beijing's port and grain depot, and then in 1860 it was forced open to foreign trade and carved into concessions. What makes it unusual is how many: British, French, German, Japanese, Russian, Italian, Austro-Hungarian, Belgian and American, each building in its own national style within walking distance of the others.
history.origins: A garrison and canal town where the Grand Canal met the Hai River, feeding Beijing.

periods.name: Ming and Qing
periods.text: Walled garrison, salt trade and grain transhipment. Wealthy merchants, no prestige.

periods.name: Concessions, 1860-1945
periods.text: Nine foreign settlements, each with its own architecture, police and rules. The city became a refuge for deposed politicians and the last emperor, and an experiment in every European building style at once.

periods.name: Republican era
periods.text: Banking, industry, and a famously sharp popular culture: crosstalk, storytelling, opera and street food.

periods.name: People's Republic
periods.text: Heavy industry and port work. The 1976 Tangshan earthquake did severe damage.

periods.name: Since 2000
periods.text: The Binhai new area, a high-speed rail link to Beijing in half an hour, and a restoration programme that cleaned up the concession districts for tourism.

history.modern: Tianjin is a large port and industrial city that has struggled economically relative to its neighbours, and it wears that lightly. The restored districts are genuinely handsome; the rest is ordinary working China. The comedy tradition is alive and the food culture is taken very seriously.
history.whyItMatters: Walking the Five Great Avenues you can read the whole nineteenth-century carve-up of China in domestic architecture: mock-Tudor next to Beaux-Arts next to Spanish revival, all built for Chinese and foreign elites who wanted out of imperial politics.
visible: The Five Great Avenues hold over 2,000 pre-war villas in a dozen national styles.
The Italian Concession is the only surviving Italian settlement in Asia.
Jiefang North Road was the banking street, and the granite facades are still there.
Zhang Xueliang's and Puyi's residences are both open and tell the story of the era's refugees.

historic.name: Five Great Avenues (Wudadao)
historic.why: A square kilometre of pre-war villas. Walk it, or take a pedicab if your legs have gone. The Minyuan Stadium end has the cafes.

historic.name: Italian Style Town
historic.why: Piazza, church and restored Italian villas. Touristy and pleasant, especially at dusk.

historic.name: Jiefang North Road
historic.why: The old banking street, a canyon of colonial granite. Free and mostly empty.

historic.name: Ancient Culture Street and Tianhou Temple
historic.why: Reconstructed Qing-style shopping street around a genuinely old temple to the sea goddess.

historic.name: Puyi's residence (Jingyuan) and Zhang Yuan
historic.why: Where the last emperor lived after the abdication, in a Japanese-built garden villa.

historic.name: Xikai Church
historic.why: A big French Catholic cathedral with three domes, at the end of the main shopping street.

arts.name: Tianjin Museum
arts.why: Regional history and a strong collection of Chinese painting and calligraphy. Free.

arts.name: Tianjin Binhai Library
arts.why: The viral 'eye' library with tiered shelving. Many of the upper books are printed on the wall, which is worth knowing before you travel forty minutes.

arts.name: Crosstalk theatre
arts.why: Xiangsheng is a two-man comic dialogue form and Tianjin is its heartland. Even without Mandarin, the timing and the room are worth an hour.

arts.name: Yangliuqing New Year print workshop
arts.why: Woodblock New Year prints, a 400-year-old local craft, still being cut and printed.

food.identity: Tianjin food is northern port food: wheat, sesame, fried dough and a great deal of humour about it. The city takes its snacks more seriously than its restaurants, and the three famous ones are treated as civic institutions. There is also excellent seafood, being on the Bohai gulf, and a strong Hui Muslim tradition.

mustTry.what: Pleated steamed pork buns with an eighteen-fold crimp, from an 1858 shop.
mustTry.why: The most famous baozi in China, though locals will tell you the fame outran the quality decades ago.
mustTry.howLocalsEat: For breakfast, and often at a neighbourhood shop rather than the famous one.
mustTry.importance: Essential as a rite, Recommended as a meal

mustTry.what: The Tianjin original: a mung bean crepe with egg, folded round a crisp fried dough stick, with fermented bean sauce and chilli.
mustTry.why: This is the source of the dish Beijing sells. The local version uses guozi, a length of fried dough, not a cracker.
mustTry.howLocalsEat: From a cart, before nine, standing up.

mustTry.what: A large, hard, deep-fried dough twist studded with sugar, sesame and nuts.
mustTry.why: One of the three famous snacks and the classic gift to take home.
mustTry.howLocalsEat: Broken up and shared with tea.

mustTry.what: Fried glutinous rice cakes with red bean paste.
mustTry.why: The third of the famous three, from a shop in an alley named after an ear.
mustTry.flavour: Sticky, sweet, hot from the oil.

mustTry.what: Crab, razor clams, mantis shrimp and small fish from the gulf.
mustTry.why: The port's other food story, and cheaper than in Beijing.

timeGuidance.three: Tianjin does not need three days. One long day covers the essentials; two lets you slow down and add a crosstalk evening.
timeGuidance.fivePlus: Only if you are using it as a base for Panshan, Huangyaguan Great Wall and the Bohai coast.

dayTrips.why: It works in both directions, and many people day-trip to Tianjin from Beijing rather than the reverse.
dayTrips.logistics: Trains every few minutes between Beijing South and Tianjin.

dayTrips.why: Tianjin's own restored stretch of wall, with a fraction of the visitors of the Beijing sections.
dayTrips.suits: Anyone who wants the wall alone.
dayTrips.logistics: Car or coach from the city.

dayTrips.why: Granite peaks, temples and a cable car; a Qing imperial favourite.

practical.gettingAround: The metro covers the centre adequately and the concession districts are best walked; the Five Great Avenues, Italian Concession and riverfront are all within a couple of kilometres of each other. Pedicabs and Didi fill the gaps. From Beijing, high-speed trains run from Beijing South to Tianjin in about 35 minutes and to Tianjin West in a little less; book ahead on weekends.
practical.whenToGo: September and October are the best: dry, mild and crab season on the Bohai gulf. April and May are good. Summer is hot and humid, winter cold and windy off the sea but the light is clear and the snack stalls are at their best.

howLong.one: Five Great Avenues, lunch, Ancient Culture Street, Italian Concession at dusk, river at night. A very full day trip from Beijing.
howLong.twoThree: Add a crosstalk show, the museum, Shenyang Dao market and a proper breakfast crawl. Two days is generous.
howLong.fourFive: Only with Huangyaguan and Panshan added.

culture: Passport needed for rail and hotels.
Payment by phone; set up Alipay or WeChat Pay before arriving.
Tianjin people are famously quick and jokey; the crosstalk tradition is a source of civic pride.
Book Beijing-Tianjin trains ahead at weekends and holidays.
Goubuli is a tourist rite rather than the best baozi in town, and locals enjoy saying so.

whatIdDo.plan: Early train from Beijing. Jianbing guozi from a cart on arrival. Five Great Avenues on foot for two hours, coffee at Minyuan. Ancient Culture Street and Tianhou Temple after lunch. Jiefang North Road, then the Italian Concession as the light goes. Dinner on the piazza, river walk and the Eye after dark. Late train back, or stay.
Breakfast crawl: guobacai, then a neighbourhood baozi shop. Tianjin Museum or Shenyang Dao market. Afternoon free. Crosstalk at a tea house in the evening.

quickRef.dayTrip: Huangyaguan Great Wall, or Beijing in reverse
